samples.summary: Blanket `Origin` header rejection can refuse the genuine browser redirect, breaking every login
samples.evidence: `if (req.method !== 'GET' || req.headers.origin !== undefined) { refuse(res, 403, REFUSAL.notNavigation); return; }` rejects any /callback request carrying an `Origin`. The genuine hit is a cross-site 302 from the backend to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>`; several browsers attach `Origin: null` to cross-origin redirected navigations (and Safari has historically attached one). If any browser in the supported set does so, the real redirect is refused, the wait never settles, and login hangs for the full 30s and then fails — a complete break of the login flow, not a degraded one. No user-agent-side evidence is present in the repo to show this was verified against a real browser.

samples.summary: CLI now hard-requires a backend that echoes `state`; against any older/self-hosted server every login fails
samples.evidence: `if (!nonceMatches(nonce, state))` refuses unconditionally, and a refusal deliberately never settles the wait. A CLI published to npm can be upgraded independently of a self-hosted backend; against a backend that predates the `state` echo in auth.controller.ts:131-135, every genuine redirect is refused and `wafflebase login` blocks for the full 30s timeout before failing. There is no negotiated fallback (e.g. accept a missing `state` only when the CLI can confirm the server is old), only a diagnostic message after the timeout.

samples.summary: A malformed nonce is silently dropped, producing a 30s hang and a misleading "server is older than this CLI" diagnosis
samples.evidence: `parseCliNonce(req.query?.nonce)` returns `undefined` for anything not `/^[0-9a-f]{32,128}$/` (e.g. uppercase hex, an array-valued repeated `?nonce=` query param, a 16-char nonce). The guard then stores no nonce, the callback omits `state`, and the CLI reports REFUSAL.noState — 'the server is likely older than this CLI' — which is the wrong cause. Rejecting with a 400 at the guard would name the real fault.

samples.summary: `--format` validation ordering is inconsistent: the dry-run branches of `cells set`/`cells delete` bypass `parseOutputFormat` entirely
samples.evidence: In cells.ts the `if (opts.dryRun) { printDryRun(...); return; }` block sits above the try that calls `parseOutputFormat` (lines 52-60 and 86-93), so `cells set doc A1 v --dry-run --format bogus` succeeds silently. By contrast docs.ts:98-105 and notes.ts:58-67 call `parseOutputFormat` before their dry-run branch, so the same bad flag exits 1 there. Same flag, same command family, two different outcomes.

samples.summary: `--format csv` now mutates values (leading `'`), so CSV taken from `cells get --format csv` no longer round-trips
samples.evidence: `neutralizeFormula` prefixes `'` on any value starting with `=+-@\t\r` that is not a plain number. `sheets export` opts out (`neutralizeFormulas: false`), but `wafflebase sheets cells get <doc> --format csv > f.csv` goes through `format()` -> `formatCsv(data, { neutralizeFormulas: true })` (formatter.ts:61) and emits `'=SUM(B2:B100)`. Feeding that file back through `sheets import` (buildCellMap writes `{ value }`) stores the literal apostrophe text. The opt-out was applied to only one of the two paths that produce a CSV a user may re-import.

samples.summary: Timeout can reject `callbackPromise` with no handler attached, producing an unhandled rejection (process crash on modern Node)
samples.evidence: `callbackPromise` is created eagerly at line 253 and rejected by the timer at line 338. If the outer promise rejects instead of resolving — `reject(new Error('Failed to start callback server'))` at line 350, or `reject(err)` at line 368 after 3 EADDRINUSE attempts — the caller never receives `waitForCallback`/`close`, the timer is never cleared, and 30s later `callbackReject` fires on a promise nobody awaits. Node's default `--unhandled-rejections=throw` terminates the process. Pre-existing shape, but the function is rewritten here and the new `options.timeoutMs` widens who can hit it.

samples.summary: An empty `state=` is reported as `badState` rather than `noState`
samples.evidence: `refuse(res, 403, state === null ? REFUSAL.noState : REFUSAL.badState)` — `?state=` yields `''`, not `null`, so a server that echoes an empty value is diagnosed as 'a callback that is not ours' rather than 'the server did not echo the nonce'. `nonceMatches` already treats `''` as absent via `if (!received) return false`.

samples.summary: Comment states a fact that is false: `bin.ts` does have a top-level handler
samples.evidence: The new comment reads '`bin.ts` has no top-level handler', but bin.ts:6 calls `runCli()`, and cli.ts:75-91 wraps `program.parseAsync` in try/catch and routes anything unhandled through `outputError`. The wrapping added here is still reasonable (it preserves per-command exit semantics), but the stated justification is wrong and will mislead the next reader.

samples.summary: Any localhost probe poisons the timeout diagnosis
samples.evidence: `refuse()` sets `lastRefusal` for every non-GET / Origin-bearing request to /callback, including harmless local probes (HEAD from a scanner, another tool on the same port). The timeout message then blames a refusal that had nothing to do with the login, e.g. reporting REFUSAL.notNavigation when the browser simply never came back.

finding.summary: Blanket `Origin` header rejection can refuse the genuine browser redirect, breaking every login
finding.evidence: `if (req.method !== 'GET' || req.headers.origin !== undefined) { refuse(res, 403, REFUSAL.notNavigation); return; }` rejects any /callback request carrying an `Origin`. The genuine hit is a cross-site 302 from the backend to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>`; several browsers attach `Origin: null` to cross-origin redirected navigations (and Safari has historically attached one). If any browser in the supported set does so, the real redirect is refused, the wait never settles, and login hangs for the full 30s and then fails — a complete break of the login flow, not a degraded one. No user-agent-side evidence is present in the repo to show this was verified against a real browser.

verdict.reason: The quoted code is present verbatim at packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:267 and rejects any /callback request carrying any Origin header, before the nonce check. A refusal deliberately does not settle the wait (refuse() at login.ts:240-249 only records lastRefusal; only the 200 path resolves at login.ts:329-332), so if a genuine redirect were ever refused the CLI would hang until the 30s timeout and then reject (login.ts:335-341) — the claimed impact chain is real given the premise. The genuine hit is indeed a cross-site 302 from the backend to loopback (packages/backend/src/auth/auth.controller.ts:134-136, documented at docs/design/cli.md:180-182). No refutation ground holds: the code is present as described; nothing guards or bypasses it (line 267 is the first check after the path match, reached by every /callback request); and a hung/failed login is squarely in the correctness lane. Whether a real browser attaches Origin to a redirected top-level GET navigation (or whether Chrome's private-network-access preflight arrives as a non-GET OPTIONS and is refused here) is user-agent behavior I cannot establish from this repository — the only Origin tests use an attacker origin (packages/cli/test/login.test.ts:81-99, 123-136), so the repo contains no verification either way. Per the rule that uncertainty keeps the finding, I confirm.

finding.summary: CLI now hard-requires a backend that echoes `state`; against any older/self-hosted server every login fails
finding.evidence: `if (!nonceMatches(nonce, state))` refuses unconditionally, and a refusal deliberately never settles the wait. A CLI published to npm can be upgraded independently of a self-hosted backend; against a backend that predates the `state` echo in auth.controller.ts:131-135, every genuine redirect is refused and `wafflebase login` blocks for the full 30s timeout before failing. There is no negotiated fallback (e.g. accept a missing `state` only when the CLI can confirm the server is old), only a diagnostic message after the timeout.

verdict.reason: The cited mechanism exists (login.ts:280-288 refuses a state-mismatched callback and deliberately does not settle the wait), but it is not a correctness defect under this lens, and a key factual claim in the evidence is wrong. (1) The evidence says there is "only a diagnostic message after the timeout" — false: `refuse()` at login.ts:240-249 immediately prints "Refused a login callback: <reason>" to stderr and returns a 403 body to the browser; `REFUSAL.noState` (login.ts:190-194) names the exact cause ("the server is likely older than this CLI — update the server, or use a CLI matching it"), and it is repeated at timeout via `loginTimeoutMessage` (login.ts:206-209). So the failure is diagnosed as it happens, not after 30s. (2) In-repo the flow is consistent end to end: the CLI sends a 64-hex nonce (login.ts:34,40,158-160), `parseCliNonce` accepts /^[0-9a-f]{32,128}$/ (github-auth.guard.ts:10-13,39), the store round-trips it (cli-auth.store.ts:30-60), and the controller echoes it as `state` (auth.controller.ts:127-136). No wrong condition, boundary error, inverted logic, null crash, dropped await, race, or data loss exists on any path. (3) What is left is a deliberate cross-version compatibility contract with backends older than this commit — a release/compat policy question, and the requested "negotiated fallback" is a security tradeoff owned by the Security lens, not a correctness fix: a forged loopback callback can simply omit `state`, so accepting a stateless callback would fully reopen the login-CSRF/session-fixation the nonce exists to close (documented login.ts:211-227, pinned by tests at packages/cli/test/login.test.ts:55-79 and 108-121). Out of scope for Correctness.

finding.summary: CSV formula neutralization also rewrites `sheets export --file-format csv`, corrupting exported formulas and any export→import round trip
finding.evidence: `neutralizeFormula` is applied unconditionally inside `formatCsv`'s `csvEscape` (csv.ts:42-52). `formatCsv` is not only used for `--format csv` display output: `packages/cli/src/commands/sheets-export.ts:46` calls `formatCsv(res.data)` to write the exported spreadsheet file. Every exported cell `formula` (`=SUM(A1:A2)`) and every non-numeric value starting with `-`/`+`/`@` now gets a literal `'` prepended in the written file. Re-importing that file with `sheets import` (parseCsv → buildCellMap, sheets-import.ts:73-81) stores `'=SUM(A1:A2)` as a text value, so an export/import round trip silently mangles the sheet's data. No test covers the sheets-export path with the new neutralizer.

verdict.reason: The code is not as described. The finding's central premise — that `neutralizeFormula` is applied unconditionally in `csvEscape` and that `sheets-export.ts` calls `formatCsv(res.data)` with no opt-out — is false in this tree. `formatCsv` takes a REQUIRED `CsvOptions` parameter with a non-optional `neutralizeFormulas: boolean` (csv.ts:40-53, 58), and the escape applies neutralization only when that flag is set: `const s = options.neutralizeFormulas ? neutralizeFormula(raw) : raw;` (csv.ts:74). The export path explicitly opts out: `formatCsv(res.data, { neutralizeFormulas: false })` (sheets-export.ts:52), with an in-code comment stating the file is the input of `sheets import` and an exported `=SUM(B2:B100)` must come back as that formula. Therefore no `'` is prepended to exported formulas and the export→import round trip through parseCsv/buildCellMap (sheets-import.ts:73-81) is not mangled. I enumerated every call site of `formatCsv`: only two in production — formatter.ts:61 (render path, `true`) and sheets-export.ts:52 (interchange path, `false`) — and because the option is a required parameter, no call site can reach the neutralizer implicitly. The secondary claim of missing coverage is also wrong: packages/cli/test/sheets-export.test.ts:9,40 has a `describe('sheets export --file-format csv')` suite whose comment states the export writes a data file, not a human render.

finding.summary: Callback server rejects any request carrying an `Origin` header, which risks refusing the genuine browser redirect on browsers/proxies that attach one
finding.evidence: `if (req.method !== 'GET' || req.headers.origin !== undefined) { 403 }`. The real callback arrives as a cross-origin 302 redirect from the backend; if any browser, extension, or corporate proxy attaches an `Origin` (e.g. `Origin: null` on cross-origin redirect chains), the legitimate code is refused and, because the 403 branch deliberately never settles the promise (line 227-233), `waitForCallback()` hangs until the 30s timeout and login fails with a timeout error the user cannot diagnose. Only node `fetch` (which never sets Origin unless asked) is exercised in packages/cli/test/login.test.ts.

verdict.reason: The quoted code exists verbatim: packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:267 refuses any /callback request whose `req.headers.origin !== undefined`, and refuse() (lines 240-249) deliberately never settles callbackPromise, so a refused-but-genuine redirect leaves waitForCallback() (line 355) pending until the 30s timer (lines 335-341) rejects and login.ts:54 throws. The genuine callback really is the tail of a cross-origin redirect chain (packages/backend/src/auth/auth.controller.ts:134-135 issues res.redirect to http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback), so the CLI has no control over whether an Origin header is attached by a browser, extension, or intercepting proxy; the check fails closed on an uncontrollable header and the only outcome is a 30s hang plus login failure. No upstream guard prevents such a request from reaching line 267, and the tests only drive the server with node fetch (packages/cli/test/login.test.ts:46,60,72,114,129), which never sets Origin, so the legitimate-with-Origin case is unexercised. I could only have refuted on the external assertion that no browser sends Origin on a GET navigation redirect, which I cannot ground in any repository location; that residual uncertainty keeps the finding. Note one overstatement in the evidence that does not change the verdict: the failure is partially diagnosable, since refuse() logs the reason (line 246) and loginTimeoutMessage() (lines 206-209, called at 338) appends REFUSAL.notNavigation to the timeout error.
